question: A 36-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 3 hours after the onset of progressively worsening upper abdominal pain and 4 episodes of vomiting. His father had a myocardial infarction at the age of 40 years. Physical examination shows tenderness and guarding in the epigastrium. Bowel sounds are decreased. His serum amylase is 400 U/L. Symptomatic treatment and therapy with fenofibrate are initiated. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?

options.opd: Separate dorsal and ventral pancreatic ducts

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Upper abdominal pain" -> "Vomiting" -> "Elevated serum amylase" -> "Acute pancreatitis" -> "Hypertriglyceridemia" -> "Fenofibrate treatment" -> "Eruptive xanthomas" -> 85%
CHAIN: "Upper abdominal pain" -> "Vomiting" -> "Elevated serum amylase" -> "Acute pancreatitis" -> "Possible autoimmune pancreatitis" -> "Elevated serum IgG4 levels" -> 60%
CHAIN: "Upper abdominal pain" -> "Vomiting" -> "Elevated serum amylase" -> "Acute pancreatitis" -> "Familial hyperlipidemia" -> "Eruptive xanthomas" -> 80%
CHAIN: "Upper abdominal pain" -> "Vomiting" -> "Elevated serum amylase" -> "Acute pancreatitis" -> "Possible pancreatic duct anomaly" -> "Separate dorsal and ventral pancreatic ducts" -> 50%
CHAIN: "Upper abdominal pain" -> "Vomiting" -> "Elevated serum amylase" -> "Acute pancreatitis" -> "Hypertriglyceridemia" -> "Fenofibrate treatment" -> "Possible eruptive xanthomas" -> 75%
analysis: The patient's symptoms and elevated serum amylase suggest acute pancreatitis. The initiation of fenofibrate therapy indicates a suspicion of hypertriglyceridemia as a cause of pancreatitis. Eruptive xanthomas are skin manifestations associated with hyperlipidemia, particularly hypertriglyceridemia. Therefore, further evaluation is likely to reveal eruptive xanthomas.
